title: Fortune's wheel
hook: Lady Philosophy: Fortune turns her wheel, and you knew she was fickle (Consolation 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Boethius in prison, and Philosophy walking into his cell with her torn robe. Your line was philosophy visits. What question did the wise visitor ask you? Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Your team wins the championship one year and finishes last the next. A stock soars, then sinks. A friend's business is on the news in spring and closed by fall. We all know the feeling of being lifted and then dropped, and we usually take the drop personally. In the Middle Ages, people drew it as a picture: a great wheel, a crowned figure at the top, someone falling off the side, someone crushed at the bottom. That picture comes largely from one book. Today: Fortune's wheel.
screen: `CHAMPIONS ONE YEAR, LAST THE NEXT.` → `A WHEEL, A CROWN, A FALL.` → `FORTUNE'S WHEEL.`

segments.voice: First, the diagnosis. In book two of the Consolation, Philosophy tells Boethius what's really wrong with him. He's not suffering because Fortune changed. He's suffering because he forgot what Fortune is. You knew her, she says. She was always like this. Her only constancy is that she changes. If she stopped turning, she wouldn't be Fortune. Second, Fortune speaks. Then Philosophy does something striking: she lets Fortune talk for herself. Fortune says, in effect: everything you had, wealth, honors, family glory, was mine, lent to you. I turn my wheel; that's my game. I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unjust when the turn brings you down. Third, the comfort that isn't fake. Philosophy doesn't say the loss doesn't hurt. She reminds Boethius of what Fortune never took: people who love him, his wife and sons still living, and his own mind, which no turn of the wheel can reach. And she adds something sharp: bad fortune can teach more than good. Good fortune flatters; bad fortune shows you who your real friends are. Fourth, how far it traveled. The image ran through the Middle Ages: carved on cathedrals, painted in manuscripts, sung in Latin poems about Fortune the empress of the world. Stoics had said much the same, that external things are on loan. Boethius gave it a picture people could hold. When the wheel turns down, you can still say: I knew this was a wheel.
screen: `YOU FORGOT WHAT FORTUNE IS.` · `FORTUNE SPEAKS: IT WAS ALL LENT.` · `WHAT THE WHEEL CAN'T REACH.` · `CARVED ON CATHEDRALS.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL TURNS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture a slow wheel turning. Now think of one turn of it in your life, recent, up or down. Something given, something taken, something that changed without asking you. Look at it the way Philosophy taught: that was the wheel doing what wheels do. Then ask what the wheel didn't touch. Who's still with you? What's still yours, inside? Name one or two. Rest there, at the hub, where the turning is slowest. The bell holds the time.
Fortune's wheel. In the Consolation, Fortune turns her wheel, lifting and dropping, and Philosophy says: you always knew she was like this. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel turns. When something goes up or down today, say it quietly, and look for what stayed at the hub. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Boethius use the image of Fortune's wheel to meet gains and losses with less surprise, turning their attention to what no turn of fortune can take.

original.note: Latin: the wheel of Fortune. The image Boethius made famous, drawn and carved throughout the Middle Ages.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wheel of fortune is a game show.
what it means: Fortune turns, lifting and dropping, and that is simply what she does; the mind at the hub is not hers to take.
what a scholar hears: Consolation 2, prose 1–2 gives Fortune's own speech (a prosopopoeia), and the image fed medieval art and poems like the Carmina Burana's O Fortuna.

notes: Fortune's constancy in change: 2, prose 1. Fortune's speech and the wheel: 2, prose 2. Blessings remaining (Symmachus, wife, sons): 2, prose 3–4. Bad fortune more useful, reveals friends: 2, prose 8. Paraphrased; confirm.
Medieval wheel imagery on cathedrals (rose windows at e.g. Amiens, Basel) and in manuscripts; Carmina Burana 'O Fortuna' (13th-century text). Confirm.
Stoic link: externals on loan (Epictetus, Enchiridion 11).
